solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Make sure gullible person’s collecting right fabric

blocks.note: to see that something happens is to make sure of it
a sucker is someone easily fooled

explanation.surface: A con artist making certain a mark picks up the correct cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The collected letter lands exactly at the join of the two words, which is why it can read as a plain run of three parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Seersucker is a thin puckered cotton fabric, often striped.

clue.text: Reasonable except when noun plays part of verb

blocks.note: save = except, as in all save one
V = verb; N replaces it in SAVE

explanation.surface: A grammar rule: fine, except where a noun does a verb's job.
explanation.walkthrough: "Except when" looks like part of the grammar rule, but "except" is SAVE and "when" just links it to the swap.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sane decision is a reasonable one, sound in judgement.

clue.text: Retired engineers excluded from training duties

indicators.note: gone back, so written backwards
taken out of the next word

blocks.note: RE (Royal Engineers) backwards; take it out of EXERCISES

explanation.surface: Former army engineers left off the drill rota.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps. Remove ER from EXERCISES.
explanation.definitionFit: Excises are duties, taxes on goods made or sold at home.

clue.text: Short nurse taking home English man left in holy place

indicators.note: a word cut short has lost its end, so SISTER drops its final R

blocks.note: SISTER (a senior nurse) without its last letter
L = left, added at the end

explanation.surface: A nurse on a short shift taking an Englishman home, with a man left behind in church.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a sister is a senior nurse. The nurse takes in three pieces, not just home, and left stays outside at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Vatican's papal chapel is one holy place, famous for Michelangelo's ceiling.

clue.text: Cold fish crossing large marsh recalled leggy six-footer

indicators.note: called back: written backwards

blocks.note: a ray is a flat fish

explanation.surface: A chilly fish swimming across a big swamp, remembered as a long-legged creature.
explanation.walkthrough: "Six-footer" suggests a tall person; it is an insect with six feet. A crane fly is a daddy-long-legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A crane fly is an insect, so six-legged, with notably long legs.

clue.text: Cycling centre generates electrical connection

indicators.note: the first letter goes round to the back

blocks.note: the heart of something is its centre; its H then cycles to the back

explanation.surface: A power plant at a cycle hub making electricity.
explanation.walkthrough: British usage: what Americans call a ground wire is an earth in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: in British wiring the safety connection to the ground takes the planet's own name.

clue.text: Macho gear periodically sent west for commander

indicators.note: at regular intervals: every other letter
in an across clue, going west is going right to left

blocks.note: every other letter, starting from the second: mAcHo GeAr

explanation.surface: Tough-guy kit being shipped out for an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: An agha is an Ottoman title for a chief; it turns up in crosswords far more than in life.
explanation.definitionFit: An agha was a military commander or chief in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Slender holy object inscribed with C and E

indicators.note: C is written into the grail

blocks.note: E, as printed, goes on the end

explanation.surface: A thin sacred relic engraved with a couple of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Only C goes inside; E follows at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mostly literary or scientific: anthropologists call slender-boned early humans by this word, related to graceful.

clue.text: Quite good anaesthetic agent bolstering singer

indicators.note: in a down clue, what supports another word sits under it

explanation.surface: A decent anaesthetic propping up a singer.
explanation.walkthrough: "Quite good" reads as mild praise; "quite" alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Altogether means quite, entirely: "not altogether sure".

clue.text: American coin is fluid capital

indicators.note: the letters are free to flow into a new order

explanation.surface: A remark about the dollar as a liquid asset: American money as fluid capital.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fluid capital" reads as one money phrase; it splits into the anagram indicator and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Nicosia is one capital city among many, that of Cyprus.

clue.text: Perform again on time after Rod returned

indicators.note: sent back: written backwards

blocks.note: RE = on, concerning, as in a memo
a cane is a rod; backwards it is ENAC

explanation.surface: A stage direction for a performer called Rod, back and on cue.
explanation.walkthrough: "Rod" looks like a name, capital R and all, but it is an ordinary rod: a cane.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym built from its parts: the prefix re- means again, and to enact a scene is to perform it.

clue.text: Northern town magazine’s covering of macabre shop

indicators.note: the letters on the outside of the word

blocks.note: Elle is a fashion magazine, with its 's
to shop someone is to report them to the police

explanation.surface: A magazine's feature on a grisly shop somewhere in the North.
explanation.walkthrough: Ellesmere Port is a town in Cheshire, in north-west England. To shop someone is British slang for informing on them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellesmere Port is a port town in north-west England.

clue.text: Scary Carol circling Charlie on long slope

indicators.note: to circle something is to go all the way round it

blocks.note: to carol is to sing; it wraps round the middle
to long for is to pine for
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A woman named Carol skiing round a friend on a steep run, which sounds frightening.
explanation.walkthrough: "Carol" looks like a name, but it is the verb: to sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Spine-chilling means frightening enough to send a shiver down the back.

clue.text: Advice Bishop Lee put out is taken in easily?

indicators.note: disturbed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking whether a man called Lee is gullible once a bishop's counsel upsets him.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that "taken in easily" is a loose paraphrase of deceivable.
explanation.definitionFit: Deceivable means able to be deceived, taken in.

clue.text: Wind last of Omega watches at the bazaar in city

indicators.note: take the final letter of each of the following words

blocks.note: ELY, the cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, opened up to take the rest
last letters: omegA watcheS aT thE bazaaR

explanation.surface: Browsing Omega watches on a market stall somewhere in town.
explanation.walkthrough: "Last of" is singular but covers every word from Omega to bazaar; Omega looks like the brand of watch, but only its A counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Winds are named for the direction they come from, and one from the east is called by the noun formed from that direction.

clue.text: Mounting agreement by the sound of it

indicators.note: judge the word by how it is said, not spelt

blocks.note: assent is formal agreement; say it and spell it a different way

explanation.surface: Growing agreement, as far as one can hear.
explanation.walkthrough: "Mounting" looks like an adjective (growing agreement) but here it is a noun: the act of going up.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: mounting a hill and making a climb up it both describe going up.

clue.text: First son observed husband’s drilling power tool

blocks.note: Cain, first son of Adam and Eve
H = husband, from genealogy and marriage records

explanation.surface: A son watching his father operate a drill.
explanation.walkthrough: "First son" is not an S; it is Cain, Genesis's firstborn.
explanation.definitionFit: A chainsaw is a powered saw with teeth on a moving chain.

clue.text: Manage spinning empty half-truths for ages

indicators.note: turned round, so the letters run backwards
with the inside removed, only the outer letters stay

blocks.note: to cope is to manage; backwards it is EPOC

explanation.surface: A spin doctor turning out hollow half-truths for years on end.
explanation.walkthrough: "Manage spinning" suggests spin doctors, but spinning simply turns COPE round.
explanation.definitionFit: Epochs are long periods of time, ages.

clue.text: Where you may get crabs and more shelled fish on delta

indicators.note: its shell, the outer letters, removed

blocks.note: char is a fish of the trout family
Delta is D in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A seafood guide: crabs, plus other shellfish served on a river delta.
explanation.walkthrough: The crabs are crab apples, not crustaceans; the seafood surface hides the fruit tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Crab apples grow on trees, so an orchard is where you may pick crabs.

clue.text: Tie small hearts to nameless Xmas card

indicators.note: without N, the abbreviation for name

blocks.note: an ace is a playing card

explanation.surface: Tying little hearts onto an unsigned Christmas card.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tie" looks like a verb in the surface but is the noun: a thing that ties a shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoelace is a lace used to tie a shoe, so a tie.

clue.text: Presenter’s prompt US vehicle at head of line reported

indicators.note: in a down clue, placed above the next piece
a report is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a queue is a line of people; CUE sounds the same

explanation.surface: A TV host's cue about an American car leading a queue.
explanation.walkthrough: Autocue is the British trade name for a teleprompter.
explanation.definitionFit: An Autocue is the screen that feeds a presenter lines: a prompt.

clue.text: Fault occupant entertaining Penny in deputy’s office

definitions.note: a phrase describing the person rather than a noun: the vice president is the one in the deputy's post

blocks.note: a vice is a moral fault

explanation.surface: A tenant with a flaw having a woman called Penny round at the deputy's office.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes in right after the first letter of RESIDENT; "Penny" looks like a guest's name but is the coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice president holds the deputy's office, next below the president.

clue.text: Blues guys alternately backing key song in service?

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting from below, so after

explanation.surface: Blues men taking turns backing a singer in a particular key.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the loose definition: an elegy is a lament, as might be sung at a funeral service.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful song or poem for the dead.

clue.text: Replacement handle missing essential part, unfortunately

indicators.note: losing its essence, its central letter

blocks.note: an alias is a stand-in name, and a handle is a name; its middle I is the essential part that goes

explanation.surface: A spare door handle lacking a vital piece, sadly.
explanation.walkthrough: "Handle" looks like a door handle; it is slang for a name.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection does the job of the adverb: saying it before bad news is the same as prefacing it with unfortunately.

clue.text: Some expel liar bleating about dots on pages

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used
turned round, so read backwards

explanation.surface: Throwing out a whining liar.
explanation.walkthrough: Read from the B of bleating back to the E of expel.
explanation.definitionFit: Braille is the writing system of raised dots read by touch.

clue.text: Long-suffering saint painting around edges of cupola

indicators.note: only the first and last letters

blocks.note: an oil is an oil painting

explanation.surface: A patient saint enduring a painting of a dome.
explanation.walkthrough: "Painting" is a noun here, an oil, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoical means enduring hardship without complaint, as the long-suffering do.

clue.text: Twisted reptile losing tail in mythic poems

indicators.note: turned round so it reads backwards

blocks.note: ADDER (a snake) without its last letter

explanation.surface: A snake that has lost its tail, coiled up in a legend.
explanation.walkthrough: "Losing tail" is apt for a reptile, since lizards shed theirs; here it just drops the R.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edda is a collection of Old Norse mythological poems.

clue.text: Who’s first seen yeti moving close to tents?

definitions.text: Who’s first seen yeti moving close to tents?

indicators.note: the letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: Asking who spotted the yeti prowling near the camp.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: an eyewitness is whoever first sees the yeti near the tents.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyewitness is someone who saw an event with their own eyes.
